rules.banned_because: Someone else's names, kept out of everything Euphonia publishes (Appendix E; setting/ip-review.md).
rules.fey_type_because: "Fey" survives only as the creature type; the setting's prose says "fae" (Book Two, What's Different). The 2024 rules' own names keep it too: Fey Ancestry, Fey Touched, Fey Wanderer, Summon Fey and the SRD's Conjure Fey (Chat, 15 November). So does a list of creature types: "any Undead, Fey, or Elemental".
rules.renames_because: The setting's own names for those planes, the first two of the Revelator's Cosmography: the Feywild is the Hidden, the Shadowfell the Ghostlands (setting/whats-out.md, wheel-and-plenum.md). The SRD's "the Feywild" reads "the Hidden".

tide: The tide follows the moon alone. From the first quarter to the last, the bright fortnight around the full moon, the Hidden are **at the flood**: strong, present and near. Through the dark fortnight around the new moon they're **at the ebb**: faint, hungry and farther off. Two nights a year are **open nights**, when the Hidden come and go as they please.

The year's halves only set when the Hunt rides. The **dark half** runs from 31 October to 1 May north of the equator and from 1 May to 31 October south of it; the tropics follow their hemisphere. Through it the Wild Hunt raids, hardest at the flood; in the light half it seldom rides. The two open nights are the dark half's first night, the **autumn open night**, and its last, the **spring open night**.

Those are the rule terms. Every border has its own names for the nights, and some keep them on other dates. The Gaels call them Samhain and Beltane, and this book's European examples use those names. Persians reckon Paristan, the pari's country, nearest at Nowruz, the new year at the spring equinox. In the Andes the earth wakes hungry in the first days of August and is fed before planting. A border that keeps its own nights uses them in place of the two dates here, and the rules for an open night stay the same. The DM says when these times are, and can rule that the tide runs differently at a place of power.
